query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The high-temperature plastic strain and toughness of Reduced Activation Ferritic/Martensitic (RAFM) steels are governed by a combination of strengthening mechanisms, including a modified thermomechanical process route that induces a high dislocation density and promotes a fine distribution of MC carbides, allowing for the combination of high strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: RAFM steel with a nominal composition of Fe-0.11C-9Cr-1.1W-0.2V-0.07Ta-0.4Mn-0.25Si-0.01Ti
generation.intervention: Modified thermomechanical manufacturing process with three stages of rolling and heat treatment
generation.structural_mediator: Multi-scale ferrite/martensite structure with heterogeneous grain size populations and fine distribution of MC carbides
generation.mechanism: Combination of work hardening, precipitation hardening, and grain boundary strengthening
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, with increased uniform elongation and resistance to irradiation-induced embrittlement
generation.baseline: Conventional RAFM steel with a single-phase polycrystalline structure
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 250-650 °C and irradiation doses relevant to fusion reactor applications
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanisms by which the modified thermomechanical process route affects the microstructure and properties of RAFM steel are not fully understood and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of the high-temperature plastic strain and toughness of RAFM steel produced using the modified thermomechanical process route with conventional RAFM steel
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified thermomechanical process route does not result in improved high-temperature plastic strain and toughness compared to conventional RAFM steel, the hypothesis is falsified

It is important that these materials can be manufactured at scale for future demonstration and commercial fusion power plants, such as the European DEMO (EU DEMO) or the UK Spherical Tokamak for Energy Production (STEP) programmes, and multi-tonne conventional production routes are attractive compared to the need to establish new process routes and supply chains, which require significant investment and time.
Currently, some of the most promising materials for the breeder blanket are Reduced Activation Ferritic/Martensitic (RAFM) steels, due to their superior thermal conductivity, relatively low thermal expansion and resistance to radiation-induced swelling and helium embrittlement,. Despite international efforts to develop RAFM steels since the 1980s, and more recently in China, Russia, India and South Korea, the utilization of current RAFM steels is limited. Therefore, it is expected that by improving the room temperature elongation to failure, it will be possible to extend the high temperature service life of RAFM steels and improve their resistance to irradiation-induced embrittlement. Therefore, excessive strain- or irradiation hardening is undesirable, while at the same time, ductility, toughening and the ability to resist cracking, e.g. at notches, is desired.
In a simple single-phase polycrystalline material, the onset of dislocation slip will occur in the grains with the highest Schmid factor, which results in load transfer to the surrounding grains and eventually through the yield transition to the propagation of deformation to every grain in the material. Subsequent work hardening can be relatively limited. This is problematic, as once the work hardening rate drops below the yield stress, the material can neck at any geometric imperfection. Therefore, as the yield stress is raised, tensile ductility and the ability to blunt a crack generally drops, which gives the well-known strength-ductility trade-off. ## Processing
A modified thermomechanical manufacturing process was developed, shown schematically in Fig. 1, to provide a multi-scale ferrite/martensite structure, expressly designed to give improved strength and ductility. Eurofer97 RAFM steel with the nominal composition of Fe-0.11C-9Cr-1.1W-0.2V-0.07Ta-0.4Mn-0.25Si-0.01Ti was used as the baseline. In addition, a steel with the same composition as Eurofer97, but with the addition of 0.25Si (wt%), was investigated, Supplementary Table 1. Si improves strength and ductility, accelerates strain induced ferrite formation, and is generally known to retard cementite formation on cooling of austenite in bainitic ferrite. After reheating the slab to the soaking temperature and breakdown rolling in the austenitic temperature regime, rolling was performed in 3 stages. In the austenitic temperature regime during Stage 1 (1150–1100 °C) the steel is unable to fully recrystallise due to the relatively high alloy content.
